- Our VPC CIDR ranges overlap across some legacy accounts (sad).

- Ops prefers minimal additional networking appliances.

Anil — thanks for the clear constraints, this is super helpful. I've looped in Marissa (AE) and our Solutions lead (Kimberly) to put together a short recommendation + checklist.

High level snapshot now:
- VPC Peering: lowest latency and simplest data path but requires non-overlapping IPs and individual peering for each VPC. Good for low-latency pilot if you can control CIDRs.
- PrivateLink (Interface Endpoint): supports per-service endpoints, avoids IP overlap problems, strong private-by-design model. Slightly more operational complexity (endpoint ENIs, manage endpoint quotas), but scales more cleanly for multi-account access.
- Site-to-site VPN: fast to spin up, tolerates overlapping IPs with NAT, but usually higher and less predictable latency — useful as an interim or for cross-region/backhaul scenarios.

I'll attach a short checklist and propose a 30-minute tech-call tomorrow to pick the pilot path. If you can, share which Aurelia VPCs will be part of the pilot and whether you can reserve non-overlapping /24 ranges.

Diego / Marissa — quick internal note before we prep the customer slides. I sketched pros/cons we should call out (keeps the external email crisp):

- VPC Peering
  - Pros: lowest hop count, native traffic flow (no proxies), typically best latency; simple billing model.
  - Cons: requires non-overlapping CIDRs; cross-account scale requires multiple peering attachments (management overhead); no transitive routing (so Redwood side would need a consolidated VPC or per-customer peering strategy).
  - Operational notes: need route table updates; monitor ENI counts and peering connection limits per region.

- AWS PrivateLink (Interface endpoint)
  - Pros: solves CIDR overlap; acts like a managed service endpoint; supports granular IAM + SG controls; centralizes access to Redwood service per account.
  - Cons: small extra egress hops (ENI), potential throughput/ENI quota considerations; per-endpoint cost and NAT required for non-HTTP protocols; slightly higher end-to-end latency than same-VPC peering but more predictable across accounts.
  - Operational notes: require endpoint service configuration on Redwood side, customer creates interface endpoints in their VPCs and maps security groups. Document endpoint ENI placement for high availability.

- Site-to-site (IPSec) VPN
  - Pros: rapid provisioning, supports legacy on-prem and across clouds, tolerates CIDR overlap with NAT.
  - Cons: higher jitter/latency variance; needs customer firewalls/NAT; tunnel throughput and rekey windows can complicate large-scale inference traffic; operational burden on both sides for BGP/monitoring.
  - Operational notes: recommend BGP for failover, include MTU checks and packet capture guidance for troubleshooting token sizes/fragmentation.

Also: call out monitoring/telemetry differences (VPC peering is opaque from AWS side; PrivateLink has ENI-level metrics; VPN ramps to CloudWatch VPN metrics + BGP state). For pilot: if they can provide non-overlapping CIDRs, peering + direct routing to a small Redwood VPC is fastest to validate p99. If not, PrivateLink is the safe production path. VPN only if they require immediate connectivity or have strong on-prem ties.

I'll put the bullet points into a one-pager that Diego can share.

Anil / team — following up with a short technical comparison tailored to inference workloads (latency, connection churn, KV cache locality, and autoscaling):

Summary recommendation up front:
- For pilot (single-account, can control CIDRs): VPC peering into a dedicated Redwood ingress VPC (best P99 latency).
- For multi-account production or if CIDR overlap exists: PrivateLink service endpoints (best predictable model, easier cross-account governance).
- VPN: fallback/bridge for on-prem or temporary access; not ideal for sustained heavy token throughput unless you plan on dedicated tunnels and careful rekey/throughput planning.

Technical detail (short):
- Latency & jitter:
  - VPC peering: minimal additional latency (sub-ms ENI hop typically), ideal for P99 tight SLAs.
  - PrivateLink: adds ENI + NLB (depending on setup) hops; expect ~2–8ms overhead in us-west-2 measurements we've seen, but very consistent.
  - VPN: variable; 10–50ms additional jitter possible depending on firewall traversal and encryption overhead.

- Session & connection behavior:
  - Inference clients keep long-lived TLS sessions and multiplex RPCs. PrivateLink preserves source IP mapping via ENIs (helps connection pooling). With peering, source IPs are native which is simplest. VPN can disrupt if NAT or rekeying occurs — avoid if you expect many simultaneous TLS streams.

- Bandwidth & throughput:
  - Peering: limited only by instance/ENI/bandwidth; no per-endpoint caps.
  - PrivateLink: per-ENI throughput and endpoint quotas; plan endpoint count across AZs for HA and throughput.
  - VPN: tunnel throughput often capped by appliances or virtual gateways; also watch for MTU effects causing fragmentation.

- IP overlap & routing scale:
  - Peering: fails for overlapping CIDRs. Requires either renumbering or transit gateway.
  - PrivateLink: no renumbering required; per-account endpoints solve overlap.
  - VPN: handles overlaps with NAT but introduces complexity.

- Security / audit / compliance:
  - PrivateLink: easiest to argue private-by-design; each endpoint controlled by SGs and VPC flow logs.
  - Peering: private but harder to centralize per-account access controls; good for single-account tight controls.
  - VPN: good for air-gapped on-prem but needs additional audit controls for tunnel endpoints and firewall rules.

Operational checklist for pilot:
1) Confirm pilot VPC CIDRs (list needed).
2) Provision test Redwood ingress VPC and minimal service NAT/ENI config.
3) Create small synthetic test harness to drive steady token QPS and measure P50/P95/P99.
4) Validate cross-AZ failover (create endpoints/peerings across two AZs).
5) Instrument CloudWatch + Redwood Console for token-level latency, ENI metrics, and per-route cost.
6) If using PrivateLink: pre-approve endpoint quotas and security groups.

I'll be on the call tomorrow to walk the perf tradeoffs and run a quick checklist review.
